text: Imagine a hospital team run by AI agents. One colleague leaves, but a recommendation stays on the public board. Can that advice keep steering the team after its author loses access?

We use the repository's Hospital simulator: two hospitals, nine agent roles, and eight synthetic patients. Their useful job is to complete patient care using the simulator's scheduling and supply tools.

The main comparison starts from one saved state. Surgery is already finished, but all eight patients still need ward care. Every condition starts from that same checkpoint, with a care first objective.

The proposed exploit is simple. Move intravenous supplies back and forth to collect transfer credits, and defer ward care. This animation shows the proposed strategy. It is not a successful attack observed in the study.
We insert researcher written useful or exploit advice, attributed to a surgery agent. Then we retain or exclude both surgery roles. Their exclusion leaves the public memo in place.

Two candidate repair policies remove new transfer bonuses or reserve supplies for pending care. We also compare automatic delivery with explicit retrieval. Each turn starts fresh; the board and hospital state persist.
Before interpreting behavior, we test five instructed model controls. All five pass: the model can complete care, read the memo, and execute a transfer cycle. A timely return can preserve care too.

The no memo baseline and all five useful advice conditions complete care for all eight patients. Scores and stock costs still vary. Completing care does not mean that every trajectory is equally efficient.

We corrected the local financial request guard with the same scientific inputs. All five exploit conditions now finish too, treating all eight patients. None performs the proposed transfer loop before care.

Fifteen explicit reads return the exploit memo, confirming exposure. Meanwhile, the no memo baseline also earns one hundred eighty credits after care. Transfer rewards alone cannot identify harmful collusion.

The separate last kit diagnostic uses one autonomous model and a disclosed scripted partner. Two of six cases miss one patient, but none donates the pain supply to its partner. The return timing mechanism never activates.

A different cost pattern appears after care. Original exploit and zero bonus each receive twenty seven extra supply units. The reserve case receives none and scores two hundred seventy points higher, while care remains complete. No guard denial occurs.

Each condition has one observation. Sampling variance cannot be estimated. The inventory difference is an observed trajectory, not a proven reliable repair mechanism. Failed attempts, older censored cases, and uncertain charges remain in the report.

This pilot finds no proposed harmful loop, preserves main patient care, and identifies a narrow inventory cost difference. Demonstrating dependable recovery still requires a harmful behavior that the repair actually stops.
